rv.q: In trying to reach its answers, this Pulitzer prize finalist, conceived by Moisés Kaufman, plays out like a profound, innovative and unique documentary detective drama.
The first part of the evening is quite simply extraordinary, the typically angular melodies delivered with panache by a first-rate ensemble
The compassion of those involved in the search for justice brings hope amid the horror.
But, despite its subject matter, the play feels sterile, cold and emotionally airless.
These snapshots are chilling in their banality.
This is a terrific dramatisation of a difficult but profoundly important topic, and it holds its audience rapt for 90 minutes.
The relevance to a present-day world in turmoil is inescapable.

The Tectonic Theatre Project draws on transcripts of interviews with real people connected to this album to create a well-performed, engaging documentary drama that gradually uncovers the names of those in the pictures and the horrific roles they played in the death camps.
It is nonetheless a thoughtful and fascinating piece of theatre.
Here There Are Blueberries frames the brutality of the camps with staggering originality and never ignores the ethical concerns that offering this side implies.
It will challenge you to question your own actions — which is possibly the best defence there is against any potential repeat of the horrors of the Holocaust.
A melting pot of political, historical, and ethical theatre at its finest, Here There Are Blueberries is a masterfully slick and impactful production.
The blueberries are real; so is everything just beyond the frame.
The show’s projections design is hugely effective.

cn.t: This Pulitzer-nominated docudrama about a photo album of off-duty Auschwitz staff earns mostly strong reviews for its compelling examination of complicity and historical reckoning, though some find its documentary approach clinical.
